1.grade_fit_note: School subjects vs language names is standard grades 5-6 capitalization; slightly easy for 6.
1.note: Clean 2x2 (Math/math x History/history) with French as a fixed anchor; only C lowercases both general subjects.

2.grade_fit_note: Capitalizing nationalities and languages is typically taught by grade 4.
2.note: 2x2 on Brazilian/Portuguese; C lowercases both proper adjectives and is unlikely to attract a grade 5 student.

3.grade_fit_note: Generic 'middle school' vs historical period 'Middle Ages' is a good grade 6 discrimination.
3.note: Well-built contrast of two identical-looking 'Middle' phrases; both distractor patterns (capitalize both, lowercase both) are plausible.

4.grade_fit_note: Agreement across a prepositional phrase plus relative clause, and 'each ... has', is grade 7 appropriate.
4.note: 2x2 on was/were and has/have; attractors (photos/grandparents next to the verb, pictures before has) are realistic.

5.note: Key is the shortest option because both errors are inserted words; a student choosing the leanest sentence gets it without the rule. A ('you will read' as a direction) is a common test-directions register, but it is still a mood shift in this sentence.

6.grade_fit_note: Semicolon between independent clauses vs comma after an introductory clause; arguably grade 7, acceptable at 8.
6.note: B is a comma splice and D misplaces both marks; A with two semicolons is rarely chosen.

7.grade_fit_note: 'ours' has no apostrophe is a grade 3-4 rule; 'everyone else's' adds a little difficulty.
7.note: 2x2 on else's/elses and ours/our's; 'our's' is a real attractor for weaker students.

8.grade_fit_note: Parentheses for nonrestrictive elements is L.6.2a.
8.note: Distractors add commas around or after the parentheses; C and D (one stray comma) are plausible.

9.grade_fit_note: Past counterfactual conditional (had + would have) is L.8.1c.
9.note: 'If ... would have' (B) is the classic spoken error and a strong distractor; D tests the result clause independently.

10.grade_fit_note: Gerund vs infinitive after stop/forget (verbals, L.8.1a) at grade 8.
10.note: Every option is grammatical on the surface; 'stopped to talk' and 'forgotten turning off' are wrong only by meaning, which is the point but makes the strand label 'Parts of Speech' a loose fit.

11.grade_fit_note: Paired commas around a nonrestrictive appositive; grade 5-6.
11.note: 2x2 on opening and closing comma; the one-comma options are realistic errors.

12.grade_fit_note: Tag question and direct address are named in L.5.2c.
12.free_elimination: A and B end an obvious tag question ('didn't you') with a period; most students reject them without knowing the comma rule.
12.note: The real discrimination is only C vs D (comma before Grandpa).

13.note: 2x2 on two dangling participles; C (fixes only the first) is the strongest distractor.

14.grade_fit_note: Quotation marks for song and poem titles, L.5.2d.
14.note: Key is the only option with both titles marked; italics are not offered so no style-guide conflict.

15.grade_fit_note: Redundant conjunction and doubled subject are grade 6-7 sentence errors.
15.note: Key is the shortest option because both errors are inserted words ('but', 'she'); strand label 'Parts of Speech' is a stretch for what is sentence structure.

16.grade_fit_note: Colon after a complete clause but not between a verb and its complement; grade 7-8.
16.note: The key's colon list followed by ', and' a second clause is awkward (a dash or a period would be cleaner), but it is not wrong.

17.grade_fit_note: Pronoun person shift, L.6.1d; on the easy side.
17.note: 'most of them take out your phones' is jarring enough that few would pick B or C; A ('you can see') is the only live distractor.

18.grade_fit_note: Subjective vs objective pronoun case, L.6.1a.
18.note: 2x2 on 'Priya and I/me' and 'she and I/her and me'; 'Priya and I' as object (C) is a strong hypercorrection attractor.

19.grade_fit_note: Past perfect for the earlier action, L.5.1b.

20.grade_fit_note: Lowercase seasons vs capitalized holidays is usually grade 3-4.
20.note: 2x2 on summer/fall with Independence Day fixed. Odd ellipsis 'every fall a fair' is grammatical but stilted.

21.note: long/windy coordinate, old/red cumulative (age + color); a few writers would comma 'old, red', but the and/reverse-order test rejects it.

22.grade_fit_note: Direction vs named region is a standard grade 6 capitalization contrast.

23.grade_fit_note: Title case with short verbs and pronouns; grade 6-7.
23.note: Chicago, MLA, APA and AP all capitalize 'Is' and 'It' in titles; 'is' is the classic trap because it is short.

24.note: tired/hungry coordinate is fixed in all options; warm vegetable and small metal are both cumulative. Key has the fewest commas, same as the key in item 21's cumulative half.

25.grade_fit_note: neither/nor pairing is L.5.1e; proximity agreement is closer to grade 6-7.
25.note: Proximity rule gives 'knows'; some usage guides (e.g. Merriam-Webster's usage notes) tolerate a plural verb with a mixed compound, so B is weakly defensible. All options also shift from present 'knows' to past 'asked', a tense inconsistency in the key.

26.grade_fit_note: Capitalizing full names of schools and parks is grade 2-3 content.
26.note: 2x2 on School/school and Park/park; clean but easy.

27.grade_fit_note: Comma after an introductory dependent clause, L.5.2b.
27.note: C and D split the subject 'storm' from its verb 'knocked'; C has the misplaced comma and no needed comma, so it reads as nonsense.

28.grade_fit_note: Paired dashes around an interrupting clause, L.8.2a.
28.note: B (commas around an independent clause) is the strongest distractor; C and D mix dash and comma.

29.note: 2x2 on myself/I and himself/hisself; 'ourselves' fixed. 'hisself' is nonstandard in every mainstream dictionary.

30.grade_fit_note: Restrictive 'that' (no commas) and comma before a sentence-modifying 'which'; grade 6-7.
30.note: 2x2 on commas around the 'that' clause and before 'which'; clean.

31.grade_fit_note: Irregular past participles (swum, broken) are grade 3-4 (L.3.1d, L.4.1b).
31.note: 2x2 on swam/swum and broke/broken; 'has swam' is a strong attractor even for older students.

32.grade_fit_note: Days of the week capitalized, 'weekend' not, is grade 2-3 content.
32.note: 2x2 on Sundays/sundays and weekend/Weekend; A (lowercase day, capitalized weekend) is backward on both and unlikely.

_batch.Spelling: No Spelling items appear in this batch (32 items: 8 Capitalization, 12 Punctuation, 12 labelled 'Phrases, Clauses, Agreement, Sentences' or 'Parts of Speech'), so the strand cannot be judged; if the form needs Spelling coverage it is missing here.
_batch.Punctuation: Almost every item (6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 14, 21, 24, 27, 28, 30; 16 too) is a 2x2 factorial: two binary decisions, four options as all combinations. That removes the 'middle option' and 'odd one out' tells, since every option differs from two others by one feature, and key letters spread A3/B3/C3/D3 across the strand. No mark-count rule decides it: the key has the most marks in 11, 12 and 14, the fewest in 8 and 24, and a middle count in 16, 21, 27 and 30. The one weak recurring pattern is that the two cumulative-adjective items (21, 24) both reward dropping commas, so a student who generalises 'fewer commas between adjectives' gets 24 free and half of 21. Item 12 has a near-free elimination (a period after 'didn't you').
_batch.Grammar and Usage: (Items labelled 'Phrases, Clauses, Agreement, Sentences' and 'Parts of Speech': 4, 5, 9, 10, 13, 15, 17, 18, 19, 25, 29, 31.) Same 2x2 factorial design throughout, keys spread A3/B3/C3/D3, and no positional or length rule overall. Exception: in 5 and 15 both errors are inserted words ('you should', 'you will'; 'but', 'she'), so the key is the uniquely shortest option and a 'pick the leanest sentence' heuristic solves both. In 17 the 'your phones' half is self-evidently wrong, which leaves a 50/50 on the other feature. Strand labels are inconsistent with content: 10 and 15, labelled 'Parts of Speech', test verbal meaning and sentence structure.
_batch.Capitalization: All eight items (1, 2, 3, 20, 22, 23, 26, 32) are 2x2 on two capitalization decisions, with keys spread A2/B2/C2/D2. No 'most capitals' or 'fewest capitals' rule works: the key has the fewest capitals in 1 and 20, the most in 2, 23 and 26, and a mixed pattern in 3, 22 and 32. The decisions are paired so that one word in each sentence goes up and one goes down (3, 22, 32), which defeats a 'be consistent' heuristic. No cross-item tell found. The weakness is difficulty rather than guessability: 2, 20, 26 and 32 are grade 2-4 content placed at grade 5.
